opus-5.5.text:
I think there are a few distinct things that could slow it down, and it's worth separating them.

The first is just that scaling might run out of steam faster than people expect. A lot of the optimism right now comes from extrapolating smooth trends: you put in more compute, more data, and the loss goes down predictably. But the thing we actually care about isn't loss, it's whether the system can do a month of coherent work. It's possible that the relationship between those two is much worse than it looks, that you get systems that are very impressive on short tasks but where the long-horizon competence just doesn't fall out of scale the way we hope. Then you'd need some new ideas, and new ideas have a much less predictable timeline.

Related to that is data. For short tasks we have enormous amounts of human-generated text that's basically demonstrating the skill. For "be an employee for a month," we don't have a corpus of that. You don't have a million recordings of someone doing a month of engineering work with all their reasoning laid out. So you either need models that generalize from shorter-horizon experience, which they might or might not do, or you need to generate that experience through reinforcement learning in long-horizon environments. That's expensive and slow, because each episode takes a long time and the feedback is sparse. If that's the bottleneck, things could take quite a bit longer than a naive compute extrapolation suggests.

The second category is economic and physical. Training runs are getting very large, and at some point you hit constraints on chip production, power, and data center buildout, and just the willingness of investors to keep putting ever-larger sums in. If we're spending tens of billions and the systems are useful but not transformatively so, you could imagine a pullback. Fabs take years to build. So even if the algorithms are fine, the hardware ramp could stall things for a while.

The third is policy and coordination. If there's a serious incident, or if governments decide this is moving too fast, you could get regulation that meaningfully slows things down. I actually think some of that would be good if it's done thoughtfully, because I'm worried about us building these systems before we understand how to make sure they're doing what we want. But it's genuinely uncertain whether that happens.

And then the last thing, which I think people underweight, is reliability. Being an employee for a month means you can't make a catastrophic error every few days. Current systems are often like a very smart person who occasionally does something bizarre. Closing that gap from "impressive" to "trustworthy enough to leave alone for weeks" might be a long tail problem, kind of like self-driving cars, where the demo was easy and the last few nines took a decade.

If I had to put it together, I'd say there's a real chance we get there within a handful of years, but a lot of my probability mass on longer timelines comes from that combination: long-horizon competence not emerging cleanly from scale, plus hardware and investment constraints biting at about the same time.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the main thing that could slow it down is just that the kind of long-horizon, agentic competence we're talking about turns out to require something qualitatively different from what you get by scaling up pretraining and then doing a bit of RL on top. Right now the systems are quite good at tasks that take a human minutes to maybe hours, and the question is whether the jump to a month is mostly a matter of more of the same, or whether there's some missing ingredient.

The most plausible missing ingredient, to me, is around learning on the job. A human employee working for a month isn't just executing a fixed policy for a month. They're accumulating context, noticing what matters in this particular organization, building up a model of what their manager actually wants, correcting their own mistakes, and so on. Current systems do that only in a very limited way, mostly by having stuff in context or in some retrieval system. If it turns out that you really need something more like continual learning, where the weights or some equivalent persistent state are being updated as the system works, then there's a real research problem there, and I could imagine it taking a long time. We don't have great recipes for that, and the ones we have tend to have problems with forgetting or instability.

A second thing is just the data and feedback problem. Training on short tasks is easy because you can get lots of them, you can score them, and you can iterate quickly. For month-long tasks, the number of independent trials you can run is way smaller, the signal is noisier, and it's much harder to tell whether the system did a good job. So even if the architecture is fine in principle, the training process might be very slow to get right. You might have to lean heavily on decomposition, on generalizing from shorter horizons, and it's not obvious that generalization will hold up.

And then there's the mundane stuff, which I think people underrate. Reliability. If a system makes a serious mistake once every few hundred actions, that's fine for a ten-minute task and completely disqualifying for a month-long one, because you're taking thousands or tens of thousands of actions and errors compound. Getting from 99 percent to 99.99 percent on each step is not a small thing, and it could easily be where a lot of the time goes.

The other category of slowdown is external rather than technical. Compute could become a bottleneck if the trend of spending more and more on training runs hits economic or physical limits sooner than people expect. Regulation could slow things down, though I'm skeptical that happens fast enough to be the binding constraint. And a serious incident, some kind of highly visible failure or misuse, could change the willingness of labs or governments to push forward.

If I had to guess, I'd say I don't think any of these will stop it, but I think it's quite plausible they stretch the timeline out by years rather than months. My honest uncertainty is pretty wide here. The thing I'd watch most closely is whether progress on longer-horizon tasks continues to track the smooth trend we've seen so far, or whether it starts to flatten out at the point where you need the system to genuinely remember and adapt over long periods. If it flattens, that's a sign one of these harder problems is actually binding.

astra-6.text:
I think the biggest uncertainty is whether the things that make a model good at a short task also make it good at a long task. You could have a system that’s very impressive when you give it a well-specified problem, but that has trouble figuring out what to do next, noticing when it’s gone wrong, and recovering without someone stepping in.

Over a month, you’re going to make mistakes. Humans make mistakes too, so the requirement can’t be that the AI never makes one. It has to be able to maintain enough understanding of what it’s doing to catch mistakes before they derail the whole project. And it’s possible that getting that behavior requires substantially more work than getting good performance on tasks that take a few minutes.

One reason that could be slow is that the training feedback becomes more expensive. If you want to know whether your system did a good job over a month, running the experiment takes a long time, and judging the result may be hard. You’d like to learn from shorter tasks and have that generalize. I expect that to work to a significant extent, but if it doesn’t, that seems like a plausible source of delay.

So I’d be looking for a situation where models keep getting better at answering questions and solving isolated problems, but the amount of time they can usefully work without supervision stops increasing. That would be evidence that there’s an additional problem to solve.

sol-6.1.text:
One possibility is that it’s much harder to train on long tasks than on short tasks. Right now, you can get a lot of mileage out of tasks where you try something, see whether it worked, and update. If the thing you care about takes a month, that feedback loop becomes much slower. And it may be hard to tell whether the model made a good decision along the way, even once you know whether the whole project succeeded.

The question is how far you can get by breaking those tasks into smaller pieces. A human employee working on a month-long project is doing lots of things that take minutes or hours, and you can imagine training an AI to do each of those things well. But there’s an additional skill of noticing that the project is going off track, revising the plan, or realizing that an assumption you made two weeks ago was wrong. It’s possible that those skills emerge pretty naturally as models get better. It’s also possible that they need a significant amount of training on the longer tasks themselves.

So I’d be particularly interested in whether we hit a regime where models look very impressive on short tasks, but getting them to reliably carry something through for a month requires substantially more experience than we can cheaply provide. That seems like a plausible source of delay, though I wouldn’t be confident that it will be a large one.
